body: The most common Hawaii licence plate is white with an arcing rainbow across the centre. Front plates are required.
Hawaii uses its own language, Hawaiian, alongside English, which is visible on many place names and signs. The language is vowel-oriented, uses only eight consonants, and every word ends in a vowel.

Hawaii has a significant amount of Generation 2 coverage, more than most US states, especially on rural roads. This older coverage is identifiable by its lower camera quality and distinct circular blurs.
Hawaii is known for its lush, tropical vegetation, including many ferns, tall grasses, and flowers along the roadsides. The volcanic islands create a wide range of landscapes.
Hawaii's topography is defined by its sloping volcanoes, rugged cliffs, hills, valleys, and craters. This distinctive landscape, combined with its tropical vegetation, is a key identifier.
Hawaiian homes are often 1 or 2-story light-colored wooden structures. A common feature is the use of volcanic rock for retaining walls.
Utility poles in Hawaii can sometimes be identified by thick yellow bands painted on them.
Hawaii's highway shields have a unique guitar-pick shape with the number at the bottom. Additionally, highway signs often use yellow signposts.
Most Generation 3 coverage in Hawaii features a visible stubby antenna on the Google car.
Hawaii features Generation 4 "smallcam" coverage, which has a lower camera position, a large circular blur, and parts of the black car are often visible. The blur can sometimes be transparent.
Raised pavement markers in Hawaii often follow a unique 1-4-1 pattern of reflectors.
Generation 2 and 4 coverage in Hawaii is exclusive to the islands of Hawaiʻi, Maui, and Oʻahu. All other islands only have Generation 3 coverage.
Kauaʻi, the westernmost covered island, is characterized by its deep red soil, large rugged hills with lush, jungle-like vegetation, and has exclusively Generation 3 coverage.
Oʻahu is home to the Honolulu urban area and features steep, lush hills visible from many parts of the island. Generation 4 coverage is common here.
Honolulu, on Oʻahu, is Hawaii's largest city. Any dense urban area with tall buildings in Hawaii will be Honolulu.
Molokaʻi has deep red soil, dry-looking vegetation, and a prominent volcano on its eastern end. It is sparsely populated and has only Generation 3 coverage.
Lānaʻi is a small island with a volcano near its center, where tall Cook pines are abundant along the main roads. It only has Generation 3 coverage.
The coastal areas of Lānaʻi are rural and feature hills with dry grass and shrubby vegetation.
Central Maui consists of dry, flat grasslands between two mountain ranges. Both Generation 3 and 4 coverage are found here.
Coastal Maui is lush and green, featuring banana plants, palm trees, and mountain views.
The interior of Hawaiʻi (The Big Island) has rolling, grassy plains, and volcanic rocks, with volcanoes often visible. Both Generation 3 and 4 coverage are common.
The coastal areas of Hawaiʻi island contain most of the towns and are more lush with trees and ferns than the interior. Generation 4 coverage is common here.
Flat, forested rural roads are common south of Hilo on Hawaiʻi island. In contrast, a mountainous forest with red soil and Generation 3 coverage is more likely Kauaʻi.
A distinct green blur on the camera is unique to the island of Oʻahu.
The "Hawaiian lattice" is a road network on the slope of Mauna Loa, recognizable by its angled roads, abundant volcanic soil and rocks, and volcanic vegetation.
Kaunakakai is the largest and most 'urban' settlement on Molokaʻi, featuring Generation 3 coverage and red soil.
The Red Hill is a unique, high-altitude location with a barren, red, rocky landscape, where clouds are often visible below.
The eastern side of Molokaʻi, near the Kamakou volcano, is hillier and more vegetated than the western part of the island.
